Question 23:
The gradient of the loss w.r.t some weight \(w_i\) in the network tells us

options.text: what direction \(w_i\) is pointing.
how large the error is caused by \(w_i\).
whether \(w_i\) is positive or negative.
whether we need to make \(w_i\) smaller or larger to reduce the error.

questions.question:
Question 24:
Parameter optimisation via iterative gradient descent

options.text: cannot end up in a global optimum.
may end up in a global optimum.
will always end up in a global optimum if the learning rate is small enough.

questions.question:
Question 25:
The loss function must be differentiable because

options.text: otherwise it could not reach zero.
otherwise it would not have a minimum.
otherwise changes to the weights would have no effect.
otherwise we could not calculate how weights need to be changed.

questions.question:
Question 26:
The learning rate is used to

options.text: control the direction of change to a weight \(w_i\) during training.
control how much overfitting is permitted.
control how close the error must come to zero before stopping the learning process.
control the amount of change to a weight \(w_i\) during training.

questions.question:
Question 27:
A single unit in a hidden layer of a FFNN, as defined above, caluclates

options.text: a linear transformation of a non-linear (weighted) sum of inputs.
a non-linear transformation of a weighted sum of inputs.
a sum of weights and inputs, transformed by a non-linear activation function.
a weighted sum of non-linearly transformed inputs.

questions.question:
Question 28:
The sum-squared-error measures

options.text: the sum of the squares of the errors a classifier will make in the future.
the square of the sum of the errors a classifier will make in the future.
the sum of the errors a classifier will make in the future.
the error of a regression model on a specific dataset.

questions.question:
Question 29:
The purpose of gradient descent in artificial neural networks is

options.text: to find the optimal combination of values for the input units.
to find the optimal combination of values for the weights.
to find the smallest values for the weights that produce an error of zero.
to find the optimal number of weights
to find the optimal number of units

questions.question:
Question 30:
If, in an artificial neural network, two fully connected neighbouring layers L1 and L2 have N and M units, respectively, then the weight matrix that represents the connection from L1 to L2 (and including the bias weights) will have

options.text: \(N^2+M^2+M\) weights
\((N+M)^2+N\) weights
\(M \times N + N\) weights
\(N \times M + M\) weights
\(N \times M\) weights

questions.question:
Question 31:
When running an ANN training algorithm several times on the same dataset, we will get different models (with possibly different error) because of

options.text: randomness in the backpropagation update algorithm.
randomness due to the learning rate.
randomness in the input feature values.
randomness in the loss function.
randomness in the initialisation of the weights.

questions.question:
Question 32:
In early stopping, we stop training an ANN

options.text: when the error on the validation data reaches zero.
when the error on the validation data starts going up.
when the error on the training data goes above the error on the validation data.
when the error on the validation data reaches the error on the training data.
when the error on the training data reaches zero.
when the error on the training data starts going up.

questions.question:
Question 33:
Binary Cross-Entropy is

options.text: a measure of influence between two binary class distributions.
a measure of information gain in decision trees in binary classification problems.
a measure of the prediction error of an FFNN in a binary classification problem.
a measure of difference between two binary class distributions.

questions.question:
Question 34:
A Naive Bayes Classifier

options.text: assumes that any pair of features is uncorrelated in \(D\).
assumes pairwise independence between classes.
assumes that features and classes are uncorrelated.
assumes pairwise independence between features in each class.
assumes that examples of two different classes have no feature values in common.

questions.question:
Question 35:
A k-Nearest Neighbour Classifier

options.text: predicts the class of an example \(x\) based on the number of neighbours in a neighbourhood of radius \(k\).
predicts the class of an example \(x\) based on a majority vote of \(x\)'s \(k\) closest neighbours.
predicts the class of an example \(x\) based on the number of neighbours of \(x\).
predicts the class of an example \(x\) based on the colour of \(x\)'s \(k\) neighbours.
predicts the class of an example \(x\) based on the distance between \(x\) and its \(k\)-th neighbour.

questions.question:
Question 36:
Which of the following statements about decision trees and the learning algorithm ID3 is correct?

options.text: In a decision tree learned by ID3, all leaves are at the same tree level.
If two training examples have the same feature values, but different class labels, there can be no decision tree that is \(100\%\) consistent with the training data.
In a decision tree learned by ID3, there can be no leaf that contains training examples of different classes.
There can be no dataset for which a consistent decision tree consists only of a root node.
In a decision tree learned by ID3, nodes at the same tree level are labeled with the same feature.

questions.question:
Question 37:
In decision tree learning, the Information Gain...

options.text: is always highest for the feature at the root of a decision tree.
of a feature that has the same value for all training examples is zero.
of a feature cannot be zero when there are still examples of more than one class in the current example subset.
is negative for all features in nodes where all examples already belong to the same class.
measures how much information a training example gives about the class.

questions.question:
Question 38:
Which of the following will *not* reduce the probability of overfitting when learning a decision tree from a dataset \(D\):

options.text: add new features that are non-linear combinations of existing ones.
reduce the set of features.
discretise numeric features.
stop splitting at a node when the number of examples in the node is below some fixed threshold.
use a numeric feature at most once along each branch.

questions.question:
Question 39:
A decision tree can overfit a given training set

options.text: only if we apply no pruning.
only if the training set does not contain all observations that are possible in the world.
only if the data contain numeric features.
only if all the features in the data are irrelevant.
only if there are errors in the training data (incorrect class labels and/or incorrect feature values).

questions.question:
Question 40:
The motivation for the Random Forest classifier is the idea that

options.text: combining decision trees into a larger tree reduces the danger of overfitting.
multiplying the input features permits more confident class predictions.
decision trees are high-bias classifiers.
more training data reduces the danger of overfitting.
combining classifiers with different errors reduces the danger of overfitting.

questions.question:
Question 41:
A Support Vector Machine

options.text: fits a non-linear decision boundary into a space of linear feature combinations.
fits a linear decision boundary into a space of non-linear feature combinations.
basis its classification decisions on vectors between pairs of examples of different classes.
bases its classification decisions on training examples that are linear combinations of each other.
moves some of the training examples apart by forcing a maximal margin between different classes.

options.text: \(kd^2\) parameters.
\(k(d+d(d+1)/2+1)\) parameters.
\(kdN^2\) parameters.
\(kd\) parameters.
\(k^2\) parameters.
\(k(d+1)\) parameters.
\(kN+d\) parameters.

questions.question:

options.text: \(kd^2\) parameters.
\(k(d+1)\) parameters.
\(k(d+d(d+1)/2+1)\) parameters.
\(kdN^2\) parameters.
\(kd\) parameters.
\(kN+d\) parameters.

questions.question:
Question 44:
The Mean Quantisation Error measures

options.text: The error that would result from quantising each feature dimension into discrete clusters (intervals).
The mean distance between any pair of cluster centers.
The average difference between mean and median of all features in \(D\).
The average distance of examples from their cluster mean.

questions.question:
Question 45:
Running the complete k-means algorithm several times on the same dataset \(D\)

options.text: will gradually reduce the MQE in each run until it reaches a global minimum.
is a strategy for preventing overfitting.
may result in a different clustering every time.
will produce the same result every time.
will gradually reduce the MQE in each run until the MQE starts to grow on an independent evaluation set.

questions.question:
Question 46:
For a fixed dataset \(D\) and any \(k<N\),

options.text: the quantisation error for any cluster is only defined if the cluster contains at least 2 examples.
the quantisation error for any cluster cannot be larger than \(k\).
the MQE can be non-zero only for even \(k\).
the minimal MQE that can be obtained with \(k\) clusters cannot be lower than the minimal MQE that can be obtained with \(k+1\) clusters.

questions.question:
Question 47:
In clustering, the Bayes Information Criterion (BIC) is used

options.text: to determine the optimal center for each cluster.
to determine the optimal number of clusters.
to determine the optimal initialisation for each cluster center.
to determine the optimal number of parameters.
to determine the optimal number of examples per cluster.

questions.question:
Question 48:
A Gaussan Mixture Model is

options.text: a probability density function over feature space.
a mixture of Gaussian (normal) and uniform distributions.
an alternative to Bayes' Rule for calculating posterior class probabilities.
a compact description of \(D\) in the form of a weighted sum of examples \(x_i \in D\).
a partitioning of dataset \(D\) into \(k\) subsets (based on random mixing of the data).
